summary: Explores why protocols need their extension and version-negotiation mechanisms to be used regularly. If a mechanism is never exercised, implementations tend to get it wrong and later changes become hard or costly. The document gives examples where lack of use made evolution difficult. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A door that is never opened gets rusty. Opening it often keeps it working.

subtitle: How protocols stay evolvable by regularly using their extension mechanisms.

tldr.problem: Protocols designed with extension points and version negotiation often cannot use those extensions when needed because implementations that never exercised the mechanisms contain bugs that make the mechanisms unreliable.
tldr.mechanism: Protocols must routinely deploy new versions and extensions in active use from the start, so that all implementations regularly encounter unknown values and learn to handle them correctly. Techniques like GREASE (reserving values to test behavior) and dependency (making extensions critical to function) ensure mechanisms stay exercised.
tldr.outcome: Protocols that maintain active use of their extension mechanisms can evolve over time; those where extensions are disused become ossified and cannot add new features.

facts.label: Solution
facts.value: Active use of extensions from deployment

today: RFC 9170 is Informational and contains guidance from the IAB. It documents lessons learned from real protocols and recommends practices for protocol design going forward. The document is used as a reference in protocol design discussions and is increasingly cited in IETF working group specifications.

sections.title: Protocol Evolution and Extensibility
sections.content:
Internet protocols need to change to survive. New use cases, new constraints, and new requirements emerge over time. The IETF has always known this, so successful protocols include extension points -- mechanisms for adding new features without changing the core protocol -- and version negotiation -- ways for endpoints to agree on which features to use.

Despite careful design, many widely deployed protocols cannot use their extension mechanisms when new features are needed. The cause is not bad design but rather disuse. Implementations built before a protocol is widely deployed may contain bugs in the extension mechanisms. If those mechanisms are never exercised in the field, the bugs remain hidden. Years later, when a new feature requires the mechanism, deployment fails because implementations break.

This RFC documents that experience and recommends that protocols exercise their extension and version-negotiation mechanisms from the start and throughout their lifetime.
sections.eli5: Even if a door is designed to open smoothly, if it never opens for years, the hinges rust and it gets stuck. The only way to keep it working is to open it regularly.

sections.title: How Disuse Breaks Protocols
sections.content:
Implementations are often imperfect. Version negotiation and extension handling code is particularly fragile because it is not exercised until the protocol is already deployed. Developers may focus on the core features first, leaving negotiation for later. When implementations with bugs in the negotiation code are shipped and deployed at scale, those bugs become nearly impossible to fix.

The problem affects multiple participants. For critical protocols (IP, BGP, DNS, TLS), fixing bugs in implementations requires coordinating across many vendors and operators, managing release cycles, and waiting for users to upgrade. If enough implementations are broken, deploying a new extension becomes infeasible -- the first operator to try it discovers interoperability failures and abandons the attempt.

A concrete example is IPv4 and IPv6. The IPv4 header contains a version field that could have selected between versions, but that mechanism never worked reliably. When IPv6 was deployed, it required a completely different link-layer selection mechanism (a new EtherType for Ethernet) because the IP version field could not be relied upon.

Examples extend to TLS, where introduction of new signature algorithm values caused implementations to break. In DNS, intolerance of the EDNS extension in some servers required a widespread compatibility workaround to be deployed before the extension could be relied upon.
sections.eli5: If the version-negotiation door is never opened during development, bugs stay hidden. When it finally needs to open years later, thousands of copies of the buggy implementation are already deployed. Now you cannot fix them all.

sections.title: Active Use of Extension Mechanisms
sections.content:
Active use means that extensions and new code points are deployed in the field and are encountered by all implementations. The more frequently implementations encounter new values, the more likely they are to handle them correctly. If an implementation handles new values incorrectly, active use will surface the bug while the system is young enough to fix.

The most effective way to guarantee active use is to make the extension mechanism critical to operation. SMTP header fields are an example: every SMTP implementation must be able to process headers it does not understand, because header fields are used for basic delivery. New headers are defined regularly, so implementations constantly encounter unknown headers. As a result, SMTP implementations reliably handle new headers.

In contrast, SIP (Session Initiation Protocol) relies heavily on back-to-back user agents (B2BUAs) in the path. These intermediaries often do not ignore unknown fields but instead remove them. This breaks new header-based features, which means SIP feature deployment is slow.

Version negotiation requires active use but is harder to achieve because new versions are rare by design. Some protocols use lower-layer negotiation mechanisms. For example, Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation (ALPN) lets each TLS connection use the protocol version that works best, enabling frequent negotiation even without TLS version changes.
sections.eli5: Make the extension mechanism a required part of the job, not an optional one. If handling new header values is required for a message to be processed, implementations will do it right. If it is optional, they will ignore it until they break.

sections.title: GREASE and Other Techniques
sections.content:
GREASE is a technique for testing extension points without changing behavior. The name comes from TLS, where a set of reserved code points are randomly offered during negotiation even though they will never be used. The idea is that implementations that see unknown values (even bogus ones) learn to tolerate them. When a real new value appears later, implementations are less likely to break.

GREASE works by assuming it is easier to implement an extension mechanism correctly than to write code to identify and reject reserved values. Implementations exposed to unknown values are less likely to be intolerant of new values when they appear in production.

Other complementary techniques include documenting invariants -- aspects of the protocol that cannot change -- so implementations know what they can rely on. Reducing the number of extension points concentrates use on fewer mechanisms. Limiting participation through encryption and integrity protection reduces the number of entities that can break the protocol. Establishing feedback systems helps developers find and fix bugs during active deployment rather than years later.
sections.eli5: Slip some fake new values into the negotiation to practice. If implementations handle the fake values gracefully, they will handle real new values the same way.

sections.title: Real-World Examples
sections.content:
Email headers (SMTP) and HTTP headers are designed identically as name-value pairs. Both see frequent addition of new header types. HTTP headers added consistently without deployment issues. SIP also uses the same design but was slowed by B2BUAs. The difference is in participation: in HTTP and SMTP, intermediaries are expected to ignore unknown headers; in SIP, they often do not.

DNS faced severe ossification. The EDNS extension was designed to add extensibility but was met with intolerance in many servers. The workaround caused EDNS to be disabled in some deployments, hiding the problem further. Recovery required a coordinated flag day where the workaround was removed, but this required enormous coordination effort and caused some servers to become inaccessible temporarily.

TCP has suffered from middleboxes that drop packets with unknown options. IPv4's version field never worked because early packet-sniffing implementations assumed only IPv4 existed. TLS version negotiation failed for the same reason: proxies would drop TLS records with new versions. Later, TLS added a mechanism to send version information in a different field that proxies would not understand, enabling successful negotiation.
sections.eli5: Email and web pages add new headers all the time and it works fine because programs ignore what they do not understand. DNS had trouble because some DNS servers refused unknown extensions. TCP has problems when routers see new options they do not expect.
